name: Intramuscular Fast-Flow Vascular Anomaly

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Intramuscular Fast-Flow Vascular Anomaly Diagnostic Criteria

criteria.description: Presence of a palpable pulsatile intramuscular mass with bruit or thrill
Imaging evidence of fast-flow vascular channels within muscle on Doppler ultrasound, MRI, or angiography
Exclusion of slow-flow vascular malformations or tumors by clinical and imaging criteria
Histopathological confirmation showing abnormal arteriovenous connections within muscle tissue (if biopsy performed)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of clinical presentation plus imaging confirmation of fast-flow vascular channels within muscle
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Biopsy is not routinely required but may be used to exclude other entities.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Audible bruit or palpable thrill over lesion
searchTerms: hearing blood flow noise over lesion
feeling vibration or buzzing on skin
detectable blood flow sound or thrill

common.symptomName: Muscle fatigue or weakness in affected area

searchTerms: increased temperature on skin over lesion

occasional.symptomName: Skin discoloration or erythema overlying lesion

searchTerms: swelling below lesion that comes and goes

rare.symptomName: High-output cardiac failure due to large shunting
searchTerms: heart failure from excessive blood flow
tingling or weakness from nerve compression

imaging: Doppler ultrasound showing high-velocity arterial flow and arteriovenous shunting
MRI demonstrating intramuscular serpiginous flow voids consistent with fast-flow vascular channels
Digital subtraction angiography confirming arteriovenous malformation with early venous filling
other: Physical examination revealing palpable thrill and audible bruit
Histopathology showing abnormal direct arteriovenous connections within muscle tissue

distinguishingFeatures: Absence of pulsatile mass or bruit
Imaging shows slow-flow characteristics without arteriovenous shunting
Typically presents in infancy or early childhood
Imaging shows proliferative vascular tumor rather than malformation

redFlags: Rapid enlargement of lesion with pain and skin ulceration
Neurological deficits due to nerve compression
references: Dubois J, et al. Vascular anomalies: classification, diagnosis, and management. Pediatr Radiol. 2018.
Mulliken JB, Glowacki J. Hemangiomas and vascular malformations in infants and children: a classification based on endothelial characteristics. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1982.
